PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 153 — Lesson 177: Reproductive, Gynecologic & Sexual Health Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate reproductive goals, pregnancy possibility, bleeding pattern, pelvic anatomy, endocrine and infectious mechanisms, contraception safety, cancer risk, sexual function, and psychosocial context to identify emergencies, build a focused differential, begin safe care, and arrange definitive follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize unstable bleeding, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ovarian or testicular torsion, tubo-ovarian abscess, severe pelvic infection, and pregnancy-related emergencies.
  • Classify abnormal uterine bleeding, amenorrhea, pelvic pain, vaginal symptoms, and scrotal symptoms by mechanism and time course.
  • Apply pregnancy testing, STI testing, pelvic examination, ultrasonography, endometrial evaluation, and referral selectively and safely.
  • Use the CDC U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria and person-centered shared decision-making when selecting contraception.
  • Integrate infertility, menopause, sexual dysfunction, breast symptoms, and reproductive-system cancer warning signs.
  • Provide trauma-informed, inclusive, confidential care with explicit partner management, result ownership, and return precautions.

Part 1 — The REPRODUCTIVE Framework

Reproductive and sexual health complaints often cross organ systems. Pelvic pain can reflect pregnancy, infection, ovary, uterus, bowel, bladder, muscle, or nerve. Bleeding can be structural, hormonal, hematologic, medication-related, malignant, or pregnancy-related. The safest approach begins with physiology and pregnancy status before settling on a familiar diagnosis.

  • R — Recognize instability: shock, major bleeding, peritonitis, sepsis, torsion, acute pregnancy complication, or airway-threatening allergy.
  • E — Establish pregnancy possibility and reproductive goals: do not infer either from age, identity, relationship, or reported contraception alone.
  • P — Pattern the symptom: onset, cycle timing, volume, location, discharge, urinary or bowel symptoms, sexual exposure, and systemic findings.
  • R — Review risks: medications, thrombosis, migraine, tobacco, cancer, surgery, trauma, fertility treatment, infection, and family history.
  • O — Observe and examine appropriately: vital signs, abdomen, pelvic or genital examination when indicated, and consent at every step.
  • D — Decide dangerous alternatives: ectopic pregnancy, torsion, hemorrhage, severe PID, malignancy, or acute testicular ischemia.
  • U — Use discriminating tests: pregnancy test, CBC, STI tests, urinalysis, endocrine studies, ultrasound, biopsy, or semen analysis.
  • C — Choose patient-centered treatment: address mechanism, autonomy, pregnancy intentions, partner care, and medication safety.
  • TIVE — Track, involve specialists, verify response, and ensure closure: own results, reassess, and escalate when the course deviates.

Part 2 — Confidential, Trauma-Informed, Inclusive Care

Explain confidentiality and its limits before sensitive questions, especially for adolescents. Ask privately about sexual practices, pregnancy goals, gender identity, anatomy, contraception, coercion, violence, and safety without assumptions. Use the patient's words for body parts and partners.

Before pelvic or genital examination, explain why it may help, offer a chaperone according to policy, obtain consent, allow the patient to pause, and use the least invasive effective approach. A technically complete examination is not patient-centered if it ignores autonomy or trauma.

Part 3 — First Decision: Stable or Unstable?

Emergency findings include hypotension, syncope, shoulder pain with pregnancy possibility, severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting, peritoneal signs, heavy bleeding with poor perfusion, fever with severe pelvic illness, rapidly expanding genital swelling, sudden testicular pain, or pregnancy with neurologic, hypertensive, or cardiopulmonary warning signs.

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, pregnancy status when relevant, glucose, and source of blood. A patient can have a life-threatening ectopic pregnancy before a definitive intrauterine pregnancy has been documented.

Part 4 — Build a Precise Menstrual and Bleeding History

Record last normal menstrual period, cycle regularity, duration, volume, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, clots, flooding, pregnancy possibility, and prior pattern. Ask about dizziness, dyspnea, chest pain, pica, bruising, thyroid symptoms, weight change, medications, anticoagulants, contraception, postpartum status, and family bleeding history.

“Heavy” is subjective. Functional clues—changing protection hourly, overnight flooding, passing large clots, missing activities, or anemia symptoms—help estimate impact and urgency.

Part 5 — Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: PALM–COEIN

For nonpregnant reproductive-age patients, organize AUB using PALM–COEIN. Structural causes are Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy or hyperplasia. Nonstructural causes are Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, and Not otherwise classified.

The framework prevents reflex attribution to fibroids. Pregnancy-related bleeding is evaluated separately. Age, obesity, chronic anovulation, tamoxifen exposure, family history, persistence, and treatment failure influence the need for endometrial sampling.

Part 6 — Acute Heavy Uterine Bleeding

Assess hemodynamics, pregnancy, CBC, medication exposure, and bleeding-disorder history. Stabilization and urgent gynecologic care take priority when the patient is hypotensive, syncopal, severely anemic, or bleeding rapidly.

Medical treatment options depend on contraindications, thrombosis risk, severity, and reproductive goals. Do not select estrogen-containing therapy before assessing VTE, migraine with aura, hypertension, tobacco, and other contraindications. Persistent unstable bleeding may require procedural control.

Part 7 — Amenorrhea

Pregnancy is the first diagnosis to assess in most reproductive-age patients with amenorrhea. Then consider hypothalamic dysfunction, PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease, primary ovarian insufficiency, uterine outflow disorders, medications, chronic illness, and menopause.

History includes exercise, nutrition, weight change, stress, galactorrhea, headache or visual symptoms, androgen excess, hot flashes, surgery, and pregnancy desire. Prolonged hypoestrogenism affects bone; chronic anovulation can expose the endometrium to unopposed estrogen.

Part 8 — Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

PCOS is a clinical syndrome involving ovulatory dysfunction, androgen excess, and polycystic ovarian morphology after excluding important mimics. Ovarian cysts are not required in every diagnostic framework, and ultrasound alone does not diagnose the syndrome.

Assess pregnancy goals, endometrial protection, diabetes and cardiometabolic risk, sleep apnea, mood, eating disorders, acne or hirsutism, and fertility. Sudden severe virilization or rapidly rising androgen signs require evaluation for an androgen-secreting source.

Part 9 — Acute Pelvic Pain

Construct a differential across pregnancy, gynecologic, GI, urinary, vascular, and musculoskeletal causes. Timing, laterality, onset, bleeding, discharge, fever, nausea, bowel or urinary symptoms, sexual exposure, and fertility treatment guide probability.

Pregnancy testing is essential whenever pregnancy is biologically possible, even with reported contraception or atypical bleeding. A pelvic examination and ultrasound are selected based on the suspected mechanism, stability, and consent.

Part 10 — Ectopic Pregnancy

Ectopic pregnancy may present with unilateral or diffuse pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder pain, dizziness, or syncope. Risk factors increase probability, but absence of known risk does not exclude it.

An unstable patient with a suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy requires prompt surgical intervention. In a stable pregnancy of unknown location, serial quantitative hCG and transvaginal ultrasound are interpreted together; one hCG value should not be used in isolation to force a location diagnosis.

Part 11 — Ovarian Torsion

Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, often with nausea or vomiting, raises concern for torsion. Risk can increase with an adnexal mass, enlarged ovary, pregnancy, or fertility treatment, but torsion can occur without these.

Blood flow seen on Doppler does not absolutely exclude intermittent or partial torsion. Strong clinical suspicion requires urgent gynecologic consultation because ovarian viability is time-sensitive.

Part 12 — Ovarian Cysts and Endometriosis

Functional cysts are common, but management depends on age, pregnancy, size, morphology, symptoms, and malignancy risk. Sudden pain may reflect rupture, hemorrhage, or torsion. Complex or persistent masses need structured follow-up.

Endometriosis can cause cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, bowel or bladder pain, and infertility. A normal routine examination or ultrasound does not exclude it. Management should align with symptom burden, fertility plans, contraindications, and need for specialist confirmation.

Part 13 — Vaginal Discharge: Site and Mechanism

Characterize odor, color, consistency, itching, irritation, pain, bleeding, urinary symptoms, exposure, pregnancy, and recent antimicrobial use. Bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and trichomoniasis are different syndromes requiring different testing and management.

Cervicitis can cause mucopurulent discharge, friability, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding. Avoid diagnosing every discharge by appearance alone; microscopy, pH, point-of-care testing, or nucleic-acid testing can improve accuracy.

Part 14 — STI Screening and Testing

Testing follows anatomy and exposure, not identity labels. Pharyngeal, rectal, vaginal, cervical, urethral, blood, and urine testing are selected from sexual practices, symptoms, pregnancy, age, and risk.

Use confidential, nonjudgmental counseling; offer HIV, syphilis, hepatitis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia testing as indicated; update vaccines; discuss PrEP or PEP when relevant; and address partners. A test is not complete until the result is communicated and treatment or prevention is closed.

Part 15 — Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

PID can be mild and still threaten fertility. CDC guidance supports a low treatment threshold in at-risk patients with pelvic or lower abdominal pain when no better cause is identified and cervical-motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness is present.

Negative cervical gonorrhea or chlamydia testing does not exclude upper-tract infection. Pregnancy, severe illness, vomiting, tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate outpatient therapy, inability to exclude a surgical emergency, or lack of response requires hospital or specialty escalation. Reassess outpatient treatment within about 72 hours.

Part 16 — Genital Ulcers

Painful grouped vesicles or ulcers can suggest herpes; a painless ulcer can suggest primary syphilis, but classic appearances are not reliable enough to replace testing. Other infectious, inflammatory, traumatic, and neoplastic conditions can ulcerate.

Use lesion testing and serology as appropriate, screen for HIV and other STIs, address pregnancy, and provide partner and transmission counseling. Persistent or atypical ulcers may require biopsy or specialty evaluation.

Part 17 — Contraceptive Counseling Is a Shared Decision

Begin with the patient's goals: pregnancy prevention, menstrual control, acne, dysmenorrhea, privacy, reversibility, frequency of use, side effects, procedure preference, and future fertility. Present the full range without coercion and respect the decision to use no method.

Discuss typical-use effectiveness, STI protection, expected bleeding changes, warning signs, medication interactions, cost, access, and continuation plan. Condoms reduce STI risk but do not replace highly effective pregnancy prevention when both goals matter.

Part 18 — U.S. MEC Categories

The CDC U.S. MEC 2024 classifies conditions for each contraceptive method: category 1 has no restriction; category 2 generally has benefits outweighing risk; category 3 usually has risks outweighing benefits unless alternatives are unacceptable; category 4 represents unacceptable health risk.

The category applies to a specific condition-method pairing, not to the patient as a whole. Use the actual tables rather than memory when multiple conditions, postpartum timing, thrombosis, migraine, liver disease, cancer, or drug interactions are present.

Part 19 — Estrogen-Containing Contraception Safety

Combined hormonal contraception requires assessment of blood pressure, migraine with aura, VTE or thrombophilia history, tobacco use with age, cardiovascular disease, postpartum status, breast cancer context, liver disease, and interacting medications.

Estrogen is not automatically unsafe for every headache or every smoker, but selected combinations carry unacceptable risk. Conversely, avoid denying all hormonal methods when progestin-only or nonhormonal options may be safe.

Part 20 — Long-Acting Reversible Contraception

IUDs and implants offer highly effective reversible contraception. Counseling includes insertion, expected bleeding changes, expulsion or perforation warning signs, pregnancy testing when indicated, infection screening, and patient control over removal.

An IUD does not need automatic removal when PID is diagnosed; treat and follow closely, considering removal if improvement does not occur according to guidance. Do not require medically unnecessary procedures that create access barriers.

Part 21 — Emergency Contraception

Emergency contraception works best as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse or method failure. Options differ in timing, efficacy across body weight or BMI evidence, drug interactions, and ability to provide ongoing contraception.

Counsel about when to start or resume routine contraception, backup protection, expected bleeding, and pregnancy testing if menses is delayed. Emergency contraception does not terminate an established pregnancy and does not protect against STIs.

Part 22 — Preconception Care

Ask routinely whether pregnancy is desired in the next year and support the answer. Optimize diabetes, hypertension, thyroid disease, epilepsy, mental health, substance use, nutrition, immunization, genetic risk, and medication safety before conception.

Do not stop essential medicines abruptly. Balance fetal risk against the risk of untreated maternal disease and coordinate substitutions early. Folic acid need varies by risk; apply current recommendations.

Part 23 — Infertility

Evaluate both partners or contributors concurrently when applicable. Consider ovulation, tubal or uterine factors, semen parameters, age, timing and frequency of intercourse, sexual dysfunction, prior infection or surgery, medications, and genetic history.

Earlier referral is appropriate with advanced reproductive age, amenorrhea, known tubal or male-factor disease, endometriosis, prior gonadotoxic treatment, or other clear risk. Avoid placing the entire diagnostic burden on one partner.

Part 24 — Perimenopause and Menopause

Menopause is generally a clinical retrospective diagnosis after 12 months without menstruation in the appropriate context. During perimenopause, variable cycles can coexist with pregnancy possibility and with structural or malignant causes of bleeding.

Assess vasomotor symptoms, sleep, mood, bone, cardiovascular risk, sexual health, and genitourinary symptoms. Hormone therapy decisions require individualized benefits, route, uterus status, timing, contraindications, and patient preferences; it is not prescribed solely from a hormone level.

Part 25 — Postmenopausal Bleeding

Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation. Atrophy is common, but endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, cervical or vulvar disease, polyps, medications, and other causes must be considered.

Transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial sampling pathways depend on the clinical situation and local guidance. Persistent or recurrent bleeding requires continued evaluation even after a reassuring initial test.

Part 26 — Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause

Low estrogen can cause vaginal dryness, burning, dyspareunia, urinary urgency, dysuria, and recurrent urinary symptoms. Examination may show pale fragile tissue, but infection, dermatoses, and malignancy remain in the differential.

Begin with patient goals and nonhormonal options when appropriate. Local hormonal treatment can be considered based on symptom severity and individual cancer or medication context, with specialist collaboration when risk is complex.

Part 27 — Breast Symptoms

Characterize mass, pain, discharge, skin change, lactation, trauma, infection, pregnancy, medications, and family history. A new dominant mass requires age- and context-appropriate imaging even when tender.

Spontaneous unilateral bloody or clear discharge from a single duct, skin dimpling, nipple retraction, peau d'orange, persistent focal change, or inflammatory findings not responding as expected require diagnostic evaluation. Do not confuse screening mammography with evaluation of a symptom.

Part 28 — Cervical Cancer Screening and Abnormal Results

Screen according to current age- and risk-based guidance using primary HPV testing, cotesting, or cytology pathways where applicable. Prior results, immune status, DES exposure, and treatment history alter routine intervals.

An abnormal result is managed by calculated risk, not by treating every HPV-positive result the same. Ensure colposcopy or surveillance completion. HPV vaccination prevents new infections but does not treat an existing infection or eliminate screening needs.

Part 29 — Endometrial Cancer Warning Pattern

Postmenopausal bleeding is the classic warning. In younger patients, persistent AUB with obesity, chronic anovulation, prolonged unopposed estrogen, Lynch syndrome, or treatment failure can increase concern.

Do not repeatedly suppress bleeding without appropriate endometrial evaluation. Sampling decisions reflect age, risk, persistence, and response—not age alone.

Part 30 — Ovarian Cancer and Adnexal Masses

Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary change, weight loss, ascites, or an adnexal mass can suggest ovarian malignancy but are nonspecific. Risk assessment includes age, menopause, family and genetic history, ultrasound morphology, and clinical course.

CA-125 is not a stand-alone screening test for average-risk asymptomatic patients and can rise in benign disease. Concerning masses need risk-appropriate gynecologic or gynecologic-oncology referral.

Part 31 — Vulvar Disease and Cancer

Chronic itch, pain, pigment change, white plaques, fissures, ulceration, or a persistent mass can represent dermatitis, lichen sclerosus, infection, intraepithelial neoplasia, or cancer. Examine rather than repeatedly treating presumed yeast without confirmation.

Persistent, changing, ulcerated, or treatment-resistant lesions require biopsy or specialist evaluation. Lichen sclerosus needs long-term treatment and surveillance because scarring and malignant transformation can occur.

Part 32 — Sexual Function and Dyspareunia

Sexual function reflects desire, arousal, orgasm, pain, relationship, mood, trauma, medications, hormones, pelvic floor, vascular health, and chronic disease. Ask what outcome matters to the patient and whether pain is superficial, deep, provoked, or spontaneous.

Management may involve medication adjustment, lubricant or moisturizer, pelvic-floor therapy, treatment of infection or dermatosis, menopause care, mental health support, and specialist referral. Avoid implying symptoms are “just psychological.”

Part 33 — Reproductive Coercion and Intimate Partner Violence

Screen privately and safely. Reproductive coercion may involve contraceptive sabotage, pregnancy pressure, or control of healthcare access. Validate the patient, assess immediate danger, respect autonomy, document objectively, and offer resources without forcing disclosure or departure.

Choose communication and contraception strategies that do not increase danger. Know mandatory reporting rules, which vary by age and jurisdiction.

Part 34 — Acute Scrotal Pain

Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain, high-riding or horizontal testis, nausea, or absent cremasteric reflex raises concern for torsion. Doppler ultrasound can help when it does not delay care, but high clinical suspicion requires immediate urologic exploration.

Epididymitis usually evolves more gradually and requires STI or urinary-pathogen assessment based on age, anatomy, exposure, and procedures. A testicular mass, even painless, requires prompt ultrasound and urology evaluation.

Part 35 — Erectile Dysfunction and Male Infertility

Erectile dysfunction can be vascular, endocrine, neurologic, medication-related, psychogenic, or mixed and may be an early cardiovascular risk marker. Review libido, spontaneous erections, relationship context, blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, tobacco, testosterone symptoms, and drugs.

Before phosphodiesterase inhibitor use, assess nitrate therapy and cardiovascular fitness. Male infertility evaluation includes semen analysis, reproductive history, examination, medications, heat or toxin exposure, infection, and referral when abnormal.

Part 36 — Board-Style Case 1: Ectopic Pregnancy

A patient with six weeks of amenorrhea has unilateral pelvic pain, spotting, shoulder pain, HR 118/min, and BP 86/52 mm Hg.

Reasoning: Pregnancy-related hemorrhage from ruptured ectopic pregnancy is the immediate concern. Stabilize and arrange emergency surgical care; serial outpatient hCG testing is unsafe in an unstable patient.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 2: Ovarian Torsion

A 27-year-old with an ovarian mass develops sudden severe unilateral pain and vomiting. Doppler reports some arterial flow.

Reasoning: Preserved flow does not completely exclude torsion. The time-sensitive clinical pattern warrants urgent gynecologic consultation rather than routine follow-up.

Part 38 — Board-Style Case 3: PID

A sexually active patient has lower abdominal pain, mucopurulent discharge, cervical-motion and adnexal tenderness, and a negative pregnancy test.

Reasoning: The pattern meets a low-threshold clinical pathway for presumptive PID treatment after considering competing emergencies. Obtain indicated STI tests, treat promptly, address partners, and reassess response within about 72 hours.

Part 39 — Board-Style Case 4: Contraceptive Safety

A 38-year-old who smokes one pack daily requests a combined estrogen-containing pill.

Reasoning: CDC U.S. MEC classifies combined hormonal contraception as unacceptable risk for a patient age 35 or older smoking 15 or more cigarettes daily. Offer safer alternatives through shared decision-making rather than denying contraception.

Part 40 — Board-Style Case 5: Postmenopausal Bleeding

A 62-year-old reports one episode of painless vaginal bleeding five years after menopause.

Reasoning: Even a single episode requires evaluation for endometrial and other genital-tract pathology. Do not attribute it to atrophy without an appropriate diagnostic pathway.

Part 41 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: Contraception excludes ectopic pregnancy. Correction: no method is perfect; test pregnancy when biologically possible and symptoms fit.
  • Trap: One hCG value locates a pregnancy. Correction: stability, serial trends, and ultrasound are interpreted together.
  • Trap: Negative cervical STI tests exclude PID. Correction: upper-tract infection can still be present.
  • Trap: Every irregular cycle is PCOS. Correction: pregnancy, thyroid, prolactin, hypothalamic, ovarian, medication, and tumor causes must be considered.
  • Trap: Menopause makes all bleeding benign. Correction: postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation.
  • Trap: Contraceptive counseling means choosing for the patient. Correction: safety guidance supports informed autonomy, not coercion.

Part 42 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Stabilize: identify hemorrhage, shock, sepsis, torsion, peritonitis, and airway or cardiopulmonary threats.
  2. Establish pregnancy possibility: test early when biology and symptoms permit pregnancy.
  3. Pattern the complaint: bleeding, pain, discharge, mass, sexual function, cycle, exposure, and systemic findings.
  4. Name cannot-miss diagnoses: ectopic pregnancy, torsion, tubo-ovarian abscess, malignancy, acute scrotal ischemia, or severe infection.
  5. Test selectively: pregnancy testing, CBC, STI testing, ultrasound, endocrine studies, semen analysis, or biopsy must answer a question.
  6. Treat with autonomy and mechanism in mind: address goals, contraindications, partners, fertility, and medication safety.
  7. Close the loop: own pathology and STI results, verify response, arrange referral, and document escalation instructions.

High-Yield Summary

  • Unstable bleeding or suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy requires emergency care.
  • Pregnancy is assessed early in acute pelvic pain or amenorrhea whenever biologically possible.
  • PALM–COEIN organizes nonpregnant reproductive-age AUB.
  • Preserved Doppler flow does not fully exclude ovarian torsion when the clinical pattern is strong.
  • PID is a clinical diagnosis with a deliberately low treatment threshold because delayed care threatens fertility.
  • Use U.S. MEC for condition-method safety and preserve patient autonomy during contraceptive counseling.
  • Postmenopausal bleeding, persistent vulvar lesions, suspicious breast findings, and concerning adnexal masses require diagnostic evaluation.
  • Every pregnancy-of-unknown-location plan, STI test, pathology result, and referral requires explicit ownership.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational. Apply current CDC U.S. MEC and STI guidance, ACOG recommendations, local pregnancy and emergency pathways, jurisdictional confidentiality rules, and patient-specific specialist collaboration.
